newsitem.title: USA: American Express fights to issue cards in banks.
newsitem.headline: American Express fights to issue cards in banks.

text.p: The government is deciding whether to clear the way for American Express to do business with the same banks as MasterCard and Visa, but the bankcard companies say their competitor wants a free ride.
The Justice Department's Antitrust Division has gathered information from both sides and is now weighing their claims.
"The division is looking at competitive issues involving the prohibition of certain joint ventures in the credit card industry," a spokeswoman said this week.
American Express says resistance by MasterCard and Visa -- which prohibit banks from handling bankcards and American Express at the same time -- is anti-competitive.

"Their objection has always been that we would be free-riding on their network," said Michael O'Neill, senior vice president of public affairs for Amerian Express in New York, speaking of the complex computer systems used for settling accounts. "We're not talking about their network. We're talking about going out over our network."
MasterCard and Visa reply it is American Express that would damage competition, dividing the allegiance of banks that now compete vigorously against American Express.

"Our network is our banks," H. Eugene Lockhart, president and Chief Executive of MasterCharge, said in a telephone interview from his office in Purchase, N.Y. Lockhart said American Express was trying to take a "free ride into the banks' customer base."
Don't look for either side to back down, because the stakes are mind boggling: $800 billion of business in the United States alone in 1995, by the reckoning of Card Track.
The Frederick, Md., newsletter that focuses on the industry said the pay-off to card companies in 1995 was $75 billion in interest and fees and $16 billion from merchants.
Until recently, bankcard companies and American Express took fundamentally different approaches to winning customers.

Visa and MasterCard are each joint ventures comprising thousands of banks. The banks compete by offering their own Visa or MasterCards, stuffing the mailboxes of Americans with seemingly endless solicitations, while they cooperate to promote the trademarks and clear each other's charges.

By contrast, American Express is a publicly held company that sells directly to customers and pays charges directly to merchants. But recently American Express decided to sell cards through banks, moving in on territory occupied by Visa and MasterCard. The reason is simple, analysts say.

"American Express has been losing market share steadily for six years," said Robert McKinley, president of Ram Research Group, which publishes Card Track. "They recovered somewhat last year but not much." The company sees banks as a way of expanding its business, he said.

Visa and MasterCard are resisting American Express's change of tactics, but not always successfully. When Visa thought about barring European banks from issuing competing American Express cards the European Union said "no" and Visa backed off. European Competition Commissioner Karel van Miert trumpeted that as a victory.

"The commission is determined to ensure that payment card markets are kept open and that access by new competitors is not impeded," van Miert said. American Express now sells its cards through several major banks in Europe.
The bankcard companies contend the United States must be judged by different rules than Europe, where American Express is relatively small.
"It's very different," said MasterCard's Lockhart. "This is a scale game ... Outside of the United States they (American Express) don't have scale."
The bankcards say American Express would drain resources banks allot to keep Visa and MasterCard robust, hurting competition among the banks for bankcard customers.
Exhibit No. 1 is Advanta Corp. of Pennsylvania, a bank that recently offered MasterCards and Visa cards that would earn points in the American Express rewards programme.

"It is using one brand to sell another brand," said Lockhart, who called the programme a trademark infringement and has filed suit against Advanta. "I believe that is a very clear demonstration of the problem that would occur industry-wide" if American Express sold through banks.
